blocks.text: Charles Darwin (1809-1882), founder of the modern theory of evolution, published 'On the Origin of Species' in 1859, proposing that evolution takes place through variation in organisms and natural selection.

blocks.alt: Four panels of small beetle shapes. Overproduction: many grey beetles. Variation: beetles of different greens, some dark and some light. Struggle for survival: the light ones are crossed out as eaten. Inheritance: the next generation is mostly dark. A note explains the example of dark beetles on dark bark.
blocks.caption: Natural selection in four steps (original diagram for this topic).
blocks.long_description: Darwin's theory of natural selection has four parts. Organisms produce far more offspring than can survive. Individuals vary, and many variations are inherited. Because resources are limited there is a struggle for survival, in which individuals with advantageous (adaptive) traits survive and reproduce more. These adaptive traits are passed on, so they become more common over generations while harmful traits become rarer. In the illustration, beetles that match dark bark are eaten less, so the dark form spreads.

items: Overproduction: organisms have far greater reproductive potential than is ever realised. A female sea star releases about a million eggs a season; if all survived and half became females each laying a million eggs, a few generations would fill the oceans.
Variation: genetic variations arise by random mutation, and no two individuals are exactly alike. Variations may be advantageous, harmful or neutral, and inherited variations pass to offspring.

Struggle for survival: because far more offspring are produced than resources can support, individuals struggle to survive. Those with disadvantageous variations die or fail to reproduce, while those with advantageous variations, adaptive traits, reproduce successfully.
Inheritance of adaptive traits: adaptive traits are inherited by the next generations, while disadvantageous traits become rarer and are eventually eliminated.

blocks.title: Alfred Russel Wallace
blocks.text: The British naturalist Alfred R. Wallace (1823-1913) developed his own, very similar theory of the mechanism of evolution and wrote to Darwin about it. When both theories were presented to the Linnean Society in 1858, Wallace agreed to credit the theory to Darwin and encouraged him to publish 'On the Origin of Species'. The book prints the year of Wallace's letter as 1957; it was 1858.

blocks.prompt: Why is there a 'struggle for survival' in nature?
blocks.explanation: Organisms produce many more offspring than the available resources can support, so not all can survive.

items: Overproduction, variation, struggle for survival, inheritance of adaptive traits.
Wallace reached a similar theory (presented together in 1858).
